title: Xanthe and the Atlas
premise: In 1917, in a fog-bound river town cut off from the world when its bridge closes for the winter season, Edmund Hartwell—a battlefield nurse who has returned home to convalesce—keeps a secret ledger of the names of common soldiers that officers omit from official reports. When the town's printing workshop, the only place her ledger can be set in type and distributed, is slated for demolition by a magistrate eager to bury his own war record, Edmund must rally an unlikely found family of printers, deserters, and widows to finish the work before the ice thaws and the law returns. The novel ends with the ledger printed and smuggled across the frozen river on the last safe night of ice, as Edmund finally signs her own name—not Hartwell, but the name she abandoned years ago—choosing to be seen at last.
about_author: Cyrus Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from the First World War. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Returning to the river town of Marlowe's Bend as the bridge closes for winter, Edmund unpacks her belongings—including a ledger of 214 names she copied from field hospitals while officers' reports recorded only their own. She tells herself it is a private penance, nothing more. Emotional beat: the uneasy comfort of a person hiding in plain sight.

chapters.title: The Town That Winter Seals
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. A tour of Marlowe's Bend in the first snow: the ferry chained, the telegraph office shuttered, and the print workshop of old Silas Crane still smoking its chimney—the only press within forty miles. Edmund watches it from the square, telling herself she has no use for it. Emotional beat: longing disguised as indifference.

chapters.title: Silas Crane's Ink-Stained Hands
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund brings Silas a letter to type for a widow and discovers he printed an illegal pamphlet during the 1886 dock strike. He recognizes something in her careful handwriting and says, without asking, that he keeps no records of what passes through his shop. Emotional beat: two keepers of secrets recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Name That Isn't Hers
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, with a flashback. The postmistress addresses a parcel to 'Mr. E. Hartwell,' and Edmund lets the error stand—as she has for six years, since she took her dead brother's name to enlist. We learn why she left her old identity behind like a coat in a ditch. Emotional beat: grief braided into disguise.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's New Orders
chapters.summary: Magistrate Aldous Vane's POV. Vane, newly decorated and newly ambitious, announces the workshop will be demolished in spring to build a customs house—and that all 'unlicensed publications' must be surrendered by thaw. He remembers Silas's strike pamphlets and holds a personal grudge. Emotional beat: cold ambition dressed as civic duty.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Reads Everything
chapters.summary: Widow Constance Airey's POV. Constance, who lost three sons and reads every casualty list aloud at church, notices names missing from the official rolls—men she buried herself. She confronts Edmund after service, having glimpsed the ledger's edge in Edmund's coat. Emotional beat: the fury of a mother told her sons never existed.

chapters.title: Two Hundred and Fourteen
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In the workshop at night, Edmund shows Silas and Constance the full ledger: 214 men erased by clerical convenience, including one of Constance's sons. Silas agrees to set the pages in type; Constance vows to find paper and hands willing to distribute. Emotional beat: a private guilt becoming a shared covenant.

chapters.title: The Deserter in the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Tom Ferris's POV. Tom, a teenage deserter hiding in the boathouse since autumn, is caught stealing bread by Edmund—who instead of turning him in, hires him as the workshop's apprentice. His young eyes are the sharpest for setting small type. Emotional beat: mercy extended and, unexpectedly, received.

chapters.title: Setting the First Page
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. The first night of typesetting: Silas teaching letterforms, Constance reading names aloud like a litany, Edmund correcting against her ledger. Tom realizes this ragtag crew is the first place he has belonged since he ran. Emotional beat: found family assembling itself around a workbench.

chapters.title: Vane Closes the Ranks
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane learns a deserter may be sheltering in town and doubles the watch, also discovering that workshop coal deliveries have doubled. He suspects Silas but lacks proof, and begins squeezing the townsfolk—cutting rations to anyone who won't inform. Emotional beat: pressure tightening like a screw.

chapters.title: What the Church Bell Hides
chapters.summary: Constance's POV. Constance organizes distribution through the bell-ringers' guild, hiding folded pages inside hymnal repairs. She visits the graves of her sons and reads them the printed page bearing their names, weeping that the state refused them and strangers did not. Emotional beat: mourning transformed into testimony.

chapters.title: The Informer's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. The constable corners Tom, offering amnesty if he names his accomplices. Tom, terrified, neither confirms nor denies—but leaves the constable's office knowing the clock is now running. He confesses everything to Edmund that night. Emotional beat: fear nearly winning, loyalty holding by a thread.

chapters.title: A Ledger Is Not Enough
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund realizes names alone convince no one; they need faces and places. She begins collecting testimonies—widows, wounded veterans, a chaplain's letters—expanding the ledger into an indictment. Silas warns that more pages mean more time they don't have. Emotional beat: ambition of conscience colliding with arithmetic of days.

chapters.title: The Bridge Keeper's Daughter
chapters.summary: New character Maren's POV. Maren, daughter of the bridge keeper, has been smuggling letters across the ice for pocket money. Edmund recruits her for the final crossing, and Maren—half in love with danger, half with Tom—agrees. Emotional beat: youth choosing a side.

chapters.title: Vane Finds a Page
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. A discarded proof sheet surfaces in a gutter; Vane now knows exactly what is being printed and by whom. He obtains a warrant for the workshop, but the magistrate's court sits only when the bridge reopens—he must wait for thaw, or act illegally himself. Emotional beat: the hunter hoisted by his own legalism.

chapters.title: The Night Watch
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, rotating POVs. The whole household works through the night while constables patrol: Silas at the press until his hands bleed, Constance folding, Tom locking the door with his body when a knock comes. Edmund reads the final name aloud—her brother's. Emotional beat: exhausted solidarity, the calm inside a storm.

chapters.title: Ice Groaning on the River
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The ice is thinning early; the window for the crossing narrows to two nights. Maren tests the route with weighted sledge runs, mapping cracks by lantern light, while Vane posts men at both banks. Emotional beat: nature itself becoming the antagonist's ally.

chapters.title: The Betrayal
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. The constable, tired of waiting, raids the boathouse and drags Tom to Vane, offering him again: names, or charges. Broken and believing everyone already doomed, Tom gives up the workshop. He hates himself even as he speaks. Emotional beat: the arc's darkest turn—family fractured from within.

chapters.title: What Silas Wouldn't Burn
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Warned hours ahead by Maren, they must choose: flee with the ledger or finish the final signature pages. Silas refuses to abandon his press of fifty years; Edmund refuses to abandon the book. They split the work—Silas stays to face Vane, buying time with his surrender. Emotional beat: sacrifice as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Crossing
chapters.summary: Edmund and Maren's POV, alternating. On the last night of safe ice, Edmund and Maren cross with the finished ledger sewn into Maren's coat, pursued by lanterns along the bank, the ice cracking like gunfire beneath them. At the far shore, a railway agent—a brother of one of the 214—takes the book without a word. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into triumph.

chapters.title: The Name She Signs
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Vane arrests Silas and searches for Edmund, but finds the workshop empty except for a copy of the ledger left deliberately on his desk—with her true name signed below the dedication. Confronted by Constance and the whole congregation reading names aloud at Sunday service, Vane finds his authority dissolving; the town simply stops obeying him. Emotional beat: courage completing its circuit.

chapters.title: Spring, and the Bridge Opens
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, epilogue. The bridge reopens; the ledger reaches London and then the papers, forcing a formal inquiry into the omitted dead. Silas is released, Tom's sentence commuted to service at the rebuilt press, and Edmund—signing her real name at last—stays in Marlowe's Bend, keeping a new ledger: not of the dead, but of the living who refused to let them be forgotten. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, and a self finally claimed.
